title: The ten-day retreat, day one
hookLine: what happens: noble silence, early bells, the breath
tomorrow: The ten-day retreat, the hard days

cards: The phone goes into an envelope with your name on it. Someone at a folding table smiles and puts it in a box. That evening, after a short talk, a teacher announces that silence begins now.
Not just no talking: no notes passed, no waving, no catching anyone's eye across the dining hall. You walk back to a narrow room with a bed and a hook for your coat.
The next sound you'll hear is a bell, in the dark, long before the sun.

teach.b: First, the silence. Retreats often call it noble silence. In courses taught in the tradition of S.
N. Goenka, one well-known form of the ten-day retreat, students agree to keep silent with each other, body as well as voice, for most of the course. The point isn't to be cold.
It's to stop performing: no one to explain yourself to, and fewer places for the mind to hide.
Second, the bells. A bell wakes the hall before dawn, and bells call people to meditation, meals and rest. The day runs on them, so nobody has to decide what's next.
Deciding is one more thing set down. Third, the breath.
Day one's instruction is small: feel the breath coming in and going out at the nostrils. Not controlling it, just knowing it.
This is very close to the old discourse on mindfulness of breathing, where the Buddha describes a monk going to a quiet place, sitting, and knowing a long breath as long and a short breath as short.
Fourth, what day one feels like, by the accounts students give: the mind wanders off everywhere, and the instruction is simply to come back.
Teachers on these courses say that isn't failing the practice. Coming back is the practice. The ten-day retreat starts with almost nothing: no phone, no talking, and the air at the tip of the nose.

how: On ten-day meditation retreats, such as those in the tradition of S. N. Goenka, students keep noble silence, rise to a bell before dawn, follow a fixed schedule, and begin by attending to the breath at the nostrils.

games.q: it's day one. you've been told to feel the breath at the nostrils, and within a minute your mind is planning next week. what's the instruction?
o: notice where the mind went, and come back to the breath.
games.why: wander, and come back. the teachers say the coming back is the practice itself.

practice: Try day one's instruction: feel the air at the nostrils, coming in, going out, without changing it or judging it. When the mind wanders, notice where it went, and gently come back to the next breath.

wordCard.voice: The ten-day retreat. A stretch of days in silence, run on bells, with long hours of meditation, beginning with nothing more than the breath. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali anapana: breathing in and breathing out, the breath used as the first object of meditation.
